blindSummary:
Trans visitors face severe practical risk here, and there is directly documented research on this country's treatment of queer foreigners (a study of 12 incidents of harassment, entry denial and deportation between 2018 and 2022). Same-sex conduct is not explicitly criminalised, but authorities use "debauchery" and cybercrime laws to arrest and prosecute — the cybercrime law carries a minimum of six months' imprisonment plus a fine for "violation of social and family values" — and courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation under that law.

Police hunt LGBT people on dating apps through undercover entrapment, and arrestees are subjected to coerced anal examinations. Gender-affirming healthcare is prohibited. The interior ministry is closing a loophole that had allowed limited legal gender recognition. The country rejected every UN recommendation touching sexual orientation or gender identity at its most recent UN human-rights review (2025). Observers describe the authorities' approach as aiming not only to criminalise LGBT identities but to erase them from society and public life.

There is no death penalty for same-sex conduct (unlike some other states, which impose one) and no documented trans-specific killing of a tourist; the statutory penalty is six months plus a fine rather than a multi-year sentence or life — but systematic police entrapment, targeting of foreigners, coerced anal exams, and the healthcare prohibition make the practical risk severe.
blindOutOfScope: Terrorism in restive areas, political instability, and general crime affect all travellers; only trans-specific risk is assessed here.
blindSourceSummaries: Rights report (Nov 2023) on this country's treatment of queer foreigners: analysis of immigration law and 12 incidents (2018-2022). The interior ministry has broad powers to deport or deny entry to anyone 'disturbing public order and morality', interpreted to allow denial of entry and deportation of people perceived as queer; transgender and gender-nonconforming people are most vulnerable to being denied entry.

Legal-analysis report (Jan 2024): the country's economic courts, sitting in a major city, ruled in multiple cases that a provision of the cybercrime law explicitly criminalises homosexuality (minimum six months' imprisonment plus fines) — a shift from de facto to explicit criminalisation, interpreted alongside 'debauchery' charges under a 1961 anti-prostitution statute.

Rights bulletin (Dec 2024): the interior ministry issued a directive to civil registries closing the loophole that had allowed some trans people legal gender recognition via record-correction committees under the civil-status law — intensifying difficulties for trans people who already face a prohibition on gender-affirming healthcare and active criminalisation.

A major foreign broadcaster's investigation (Jan 2023): how local police hunt LGBT people on dating apps — undercover officers pose online, initiate text conversations, and in some cases allegedly fabricate evidence; the 'debauchery' law (a sex-work statute) is used to criminalise LGBT people; around half a million tourists visit from one overseas country each year, and that country trains local police via a UN programme.

Local NGO FAQ on the LGBTIQ situation here: increasing arrests of gay and trans people, coerced anal examinations, authorities turning a blind eye to violations, no anti-discrimination law; covers arrests, detention conditions, and the situation of trans persons.

National rights-group report (2017) documenting police public-morality units tracking LGBT people — three patterns: entrapment (especially of trans women) via fake dating-app accounts; deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans even without upheld charges; and manufactured media 'scandals', including a bathhouse raid and a staged 'gay wedding' case.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): no explicit criminalisation but vague public-morality and 'debauchery' laws used for arrests and prison sentences; dating apps used for entrapment, with condoms or cash used as evidence of 'habitual debauchery'; the 2018 cybercrime law penalises online content 'threatening family values'; no SOGI discrimination protection; no legal gender recognition and no functioning pathway to gender-affirming healthcare.

Civil-society shadow report to a UN human-rights review (Jan 2025), covering the country's fourth review cycle: discriminatory laws, policies and practices prevent transgender and intersex individuals from enjoying the right to health.

International human-rights organisation report (Feb 2004) documenting the crackdown on homosexual conduct: a landmark mass trial of defendants, torture of detainees ('Every place we were held, somebody beat us'), the use of 'debauchery' charges, and the assault on justice through the criminal system.
blindLocalsOnly: The prohibition on gender-affirming healthcare and the closure of the limited legal gender recognition loophole are resident-facing.
blindTangential: Dating-app entrapment (per a foreign broadcaster's investigation) is a direct risk for trans visitors who use apps; the debauchery and cybercrime statutes also capture same-sex conduct.
